## Proof

**Claim.** Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity satisfying the ascending chain condition (ACC) on ideals. Then every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists an ideal $I \subseteq R$ which is not finitely generated. In particular $I \neq (0) = R\cdot 0$, so $I \neq \{0\}$ is not generated by the empty set; pick any $a_1 \in I$, $a_1 \neq 0$. Then $(a_1) \subsetneq I$, since $I$ is not principal (a principal ideal is finitely generated). Choose $a_2 \in I \setminus (a_1)$; then
$$(a_1) \subsetneq (a_1, a_2).$$
Since $(a_1,a_2)$ is finitely generated and $I$ is not, $(a_1,a_2) \subsetneq I$. Choose $a_3 \in I \setminus (a_1,a_2)$, giving
$$(a_1) \subsetneq (a_1,a_2) \subsetneq (a_1,a_2,a_3).$$

Proceeding inductively: having constructed $a_1,\dots,a_n \in I$ with
$$(a_1) \subsetneq (a_1,a_2) \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq (a_1,\dots,a_n) \subseteq I,$$
the ideal $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ is finitely generated, hence strictly contained in $I$ (as $I$ is not finitely generated). Pick $a_{n+1} \in I \setminus (a_1,\dots,a_n)$, yielding
$$(a_1,\dots,a_n) \subsetneq (a_1,\dots,a_n,a_{n+1}).$$

This produces a strictly ascending chain of ideals
$$(a_1) \subsetneq (a_1,a_2) \subsetneq (a_1,a_2,a_3) \subsetneq \cdots$$
which never stabilizes — contradicting ACC.

Therefore no such $I$ exists; every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated. $\blacksquare$

---

**Remark (the converse direction, for completeness).** The converse — "every ideal finitely generated $\Rightarrow$ ACC" — also holds: given an ascending chain $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$, the union $I = \bigcup_k I_k$ is an ideal (using that the chain is totally ordered), hence finitely generated, say $I = (x_1,\dots,x_m)$. Each $x_j$ lies in some $I_{k_j}$; with $N = \max_j k_j$, all $x_j \in I_N$, so $I \subseteq I_N \subseteq I$, giving $I_N = I$ and the chain stabilizes at $N$. Thus the two conditions are equivalent — this is the standard characterization of a Noetherian ring.

### PROOF COMPLETE
